chapter.title: Plan the route

cards.body: Picture leading three friends from the car park to a lighthouse. You point at it first: "We're going there." Then you walk the path in **3 stretches, with a clear turn between each**. When you reach the lighthouse, you say "Here it is." Nobody has to guess where they are, and nobody is counting their steps.
cards.simpler: Imagine you're leading three friends from the car park to a lighthouse. First you point at it and say, "We're going there." Then you walk the path in **three stretches, with a clear turn between each one**. When you arrive, you say, "Here it is." Nobody has to guess where they are on the way, and nobody has to count their steps.

cards.prompt: You're leading the lighthouse walk. Which guide would your friends thank you for?

options.text: Point at the lighthouse, walk the path in 3 stretches, then say "Here it is" when you arrive.
Set off fast with no word about where you're going, and keep walking until everyone is tired.
Say "Lighthouse!" and then describe 9 different side paths in loving detail.

whyNot.b: That's a walk with no destination named: nobody knows where they're going, so nobody can follow. Say it first.
whyNot.c: That's one destination with 9 steps, not 3. People lose the path somewhere around step 4.

cards.reteach: A short talk has one shape: say where you're going, go there in 3 steps, say where you've arrived. Three steps is enough for a listener to hold in their head. Name the destination at both ends so nobody feels lost.

cards.title: Three parts, one card
cards.body:
A 3-minute talk has **3 parts: opening line, 3 steps, closing line**. The opening line is your one sentence from chapter 1, said straight out. It tells people where the walk ends.

The 3 steps are the route. Each one is a reason, an example or a stage that moves the listener closer to that sentence. Give each step a short name of 2 to 5 words so you can remember it.

It all fits on one *index card*, a small piece of card about the size of your palm. If it doesn't fit, you have too much.
cards.simpler:
A 3-minute talk has **three parts: an opening line, three steps, and a closing line**. The opening line is your one sentence from chapter 1, said plainly. It tells people where you'll end up.

The three steps are the path. Each is a reason, an example, or a stage. Give each a short name of 2 to 5 words.

It fits on one index card, about the size of your palm. If it won't fit, you have too much.

cards.title: Dev's card for the running club
cards.body: Dev has 3 minutes to persuade 8 colleagues to join a lunchtime running club. His one sentence: "A 20-minute run at lunch makes the afternoon easier." His 3 steps, written on the card: "1. Sleepy 2pm meetings. 2. Tried it for 4 weeks. 3. Starts Tuesday, meet at the lifts." His closing line is the same sentence again, said slower. The card has 23 words on it. He gets 5 sign-ups and one person who asks about the lifts.
cards.simpler: Dev has 3 minutes to persuade 8 colleagues to join a lunchtime running club. His one sentence is: "A 20-minute run at lunch makes the afternoon easier." On his card he writes 3 steps: "1. Sleepy 2pm meetings. 2. Tried it for 4 weeks. 3. Starts Tuesday, meet at the lifts." His closing line is the same sentence again, said more slowly. The whole card holds 23 words. He gets 5 sign-ups, and one person asks about the lifts.

cards.prompt: Priya is planning a 3-minute talk telling her book club why they should read shorter novels. Which plan follows the 3-part shape?

options.text: Open with 2 minutes of why she loves reading, then list 6 short novels, then stop when time runs out.
Open with her one sentence, then list 3 short novels, then say "Anyway, lots of good ones out there."

Open: "Short novels get finished, and finished books are the ones we talk about." Steps: 1. Half our picks go unfinished. 2. Her 3 short favourites. 3. Try one for next month. Close with the same sentence.

whyNot.a: That's a route with no destination named and no arrival, just steps until the clock stops. The opening line is missing, and so is the close.
whyNot.b: That's a good opening and 3 steps, but the close drifts away instead of landing. The closing line should be the destination, not a shrug.

cards.reteach: Check for all 3 parts: an opening line that names the point, exactly 3 steps that lead to it, and a closing line that says the point again. If any part is missing or vague, the walk has no clear start or finish.

cards.title: Why the ends match
cards.body:
Your opening line and closing line are **the same sentence, said twice**. That feels like cheating when you write it. In the room it feels like arriving. Listeners hear it first as a promise and last as proof.

The 3 steps need to go in an order a listener can feel. Dev went problem, then test, then invitation. Priya went problem, then examples, then ask. Problem first, ask last, works for most short talks.

If a step doesn't push toward the closing sentence, cut it. It's a side path. You'll want to keep it. Don't.
cards.simpler:
Your opening line and closing line are **the same sentence, said twice**. On paper that feels like cheating. In the room it feels like arriving. People hear it first as a promise and last as proof.

Put your 3 steps in an order a listener can feel. Dev went problem, test, invitation. Problem first and ask last suits most short talks.

If a step doesn't push toward the closing sentence, cut it. You'll want to keep it. Don't.

cards.body: Marcus writes his card at 11pm: opening line, then 7 steps, each with 2 sub-points. He tells himself they're all important. On the day he reaches step 4 at the 3-minute mark and finishes in a rush, skipping his closing line. You can spot this before it happens: if your card has more than 3 numbered steps, or you need a second card, you have planned a 10-minute walk for a 3-minute slot.
cards.simpler: Marcus writes his card at 11pm. He writes his opening line, then 7 steps, each with 2 smaller points. He tells himself they all matter. On the day, he reaches step 4 as the 3 minutes run out. He finishes in a rush and skips his closing line. You can spot this coming. If your card has more than 3 numbered steps, or you need a second card, you have planned a 10-minute walk for a 3-minute slot.

cards.prompt: A friend hands you their index card for a 3-minute talk. What should be on it?

options.text: The full script written out, word for word, in small handwriting.
One opening sentence, 3 named steps, and a closing sentence that matches the opening.
The 3 steps only. The opening and closing can be improvised, since they're the easy parts.

whyNot.a: That's a script, not a route. A card holds the shape of the walk, not every word of it.
whyNot.c: That's the route without the destination at either end. The opening and closing sentences are the parts people remember, so they get planned first.

cards.reteach: The index card holds 3 parts: the one sentence at the top, 3 short step names in the middle, and the same sentence at the bottom. Around 20 to 30 words in total. It's a map of the walk, not the walk itself.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A short talk is **say where you're going, go there in 3 steps, say you've arrived**. Write all 3 parts on one index card, and if it spills over, you've planned too much.
cards.simpler: A short talk is **say where you're going, go there in 3 steps, say you've arrived**. That's the whole shape. Write all 3 parts on one index card, a card about the size of your palm. If the words spill over the edge, you have planned too much for the time you have.

cards.body: Take your one sentence from chapter 1. On a card or your phone notes, write it at the top, 3 steps of 2 to 5 words each, then the sentence again at the bottom. Read it aloud once.
cards.simpler: Take the one sentence you wrote in chapter 1. On an index card, or in the notes app on your phone, write that sentence at the top. Under it, write 3 steps of 2 to 5 words each. At the bottom, write the sentence again. Then read the whole card aloud once.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now lay out a 3-minute talk on one index card with an opening line, 3 steps and a closing line.
